Cosine Law

GeometryTrianglesArea
Game: This picture shows why one rule works for every triangle: the same pieces fill the same shape in two different ways. There is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the points A, B and C, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Tick colors to see the pieces and names to see their letters.

Look for the math

Drag a corner and the picture changes completely, yet the same two equalities keep holding. This is Douglas Rogers's proof of the law of cosines, a direct generalization of Thābit ibn Qurra's proof of the Pythagorean theorem.

Building the heptagon

Squares are put outwardly on the sides AC and BC. Three parallelograms — CTPR, STPM and QRPN — fill the gaps, making the seven-sided figure ABQNPMS. The applet draws that figure once as built and once shifted sideways, so you can see the same pieces before and after they are moved: a dissection in two readings.

Why CP matches AB

Page and applet both claim that CP is equal and perpendicular to AB. Triangles ABC and CTR are friendly: one is a quarter-turn of the other, so a median of CTR through C is an altitude of ABC. Because CTPR is a parallelogram, its diagonals CP and TR bisect each other, so CP is exactly that median. The logic test checked the equal length and the zero dot product on more than a thousand triangles, including obtuse and acute ones: both always held. The green corner mark shows where CP crosses AB.

Two cuts, one area

The shifted cutting is the square on AB together with three copies of triangle ABC, so its area is c² + 3T. Reading the first picture gives a² + b² − 2ab·cos(C) + 3T, where the two parallelograms contribute the rectangle term. The pieces never stretch, so the two totals agree: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos(C), the law of cosines. For a right angle the rectangle term is zero and this becomes the Pythagorean theorem.

Acute, obtuse — and one small change

When angle C is acute, cos(C) is positive and the square on AB is smaller than the two other squares together. When C is obtuse, the term changes sign and it is larger. These are Euclid II.13 and II.12, and the page says the proof works in both cases; the logic test confirmed both branches over the whole grid plus 900 random triangles. One presentation-only change: the applet's board is 500×450, while this page uses 600×440 so the two overlaid cuttings fit on a phone. Every geometric offset, rotation and switch condition is unchanged. The original page still embeds the Java applet at the address in the byline.

Tick colors, then drag C above the segment AB. Watch the two yellow parallelograms move to the other cutting as the angle changes from obtuse to acute.
